title: The case for an older Giza
about: The guided tour: each stop names a station, the eras it runs through in order (the first is shown on arrival, the rest glided to in turn), and where the view turns (degrees: yaw from north, pitch above the horizon, vertical field of view). Figures in `numbers` are the project's own, from docs/dossier.md, docs/shafts.md and the sky page; the arguments are the proponents', put at their strongest.

stops.summary: The plateau runs back from today to 10,500 BCE, and the case is set out.
stops.title: The case for an older Giza
text: The record dates the Giza plateau to Egypt's Fourth Dynasty: Khufu's pyramid around 2560 BCE, Khafre's pyramid and the Sphinx a generation later.

A line of researchers, among them John Anthony West, the geologist Robert Schoch, Robert Bauval and Graham Hancock, argue that the plateau is much older than that: that its plan, its alignments and some of its stones belong to a forgotten age around 10,500 BCE. They identify it with Zep Tepi, the First Time, the Egyptians' own name for the age when the gods ruled the land.
This tour lays out their case at its strongest, one station at a time, with the project's own measurements beside each argument. Watch the plateau run back from today to the First Time.
stops.who: West, Serpent in the Sky (1979) · Hancock, Fingerprints of the Gods (1995) · Hancock and Bauval, Keeper of Genesis (1996)

stops.summary: Schoch's geology: the Sphinx's body worn by rain, not wind.
stops.title: Weathered by rain
text: The Sphinx is carved out of the bedrock, and the ditch around it is the quarry it came from. Look along its flank: the softer layers of rock are worn back into deep, rounded hollows, and the walls of the ditch are cut by vertical fissures.

In 1991 the Boston University geologist Robert Schoch told the Geological Society of America that this is the mark of rain running down rock for a very long time, not of wind-blown sand. Egypt's last long wet phase ended thousands of years before Khafre. If rain did this work, the Sphinx was already old when he came to the throne.

Seismic soundings that Schoch made with Thomas Dobecki found the weathering under the floor of the ditch deeper in front of the Sphinx than behind it, which he read as the front being cut first, long before the rest. Watch the body as the long rains wear it.
stops.numbers: Schoch's 1992 estimate for the carving of the Sphinx's core body: 7000 to 5000 BCE at the latest. West and Hancock argue for the eleventh millennium BCE.
stops.who: Schoch, Redating the Great Sphinx of Giza, KMT (1992) · Dobecki and Schoch, Geoarchaeology (1992) · West (1979)

stops.summary: Why the king's face may be a recut of something older.
stops.title: A head too small for its body
text: From the east the Sphinx's head is small, out of proportion with its long body. West and others read this as a recutting: a king's face of Khafre's time carved out of an older, larger head.

Hancock and Bauval go further. The body, they argue, was a lion's from the start, gazing due east, and only took a pharaoh's head when the Egyptians restored it. At the next stop you will see that lion.

stops.summary: Hundred-tonne blocks from the Sphinx's ditch, faced later in granite.
stops.title: Megaliths from the Sphinx's own quarry
text: Beside the Sphinx stands Khafre's valley temple. Its walls are built of limestone blocks cut from the Sphinx's ditch, some of them estimated at over a hundred tonnes; Hancock puts the largest at two hundred. They were later faced with polished red granite brought down the Nile from Aswan.

Schoch and West argue that the limestone behind the granite carries the same rain weathering as the ditch walls, and that the granite was cut on its back to fit the worn surfaces. On that reading the temple's core was already standing and weathered when Khafre's builders faced it.

stops.summary: The lion looking at the dawn of the Age of Leo.
stops.title: The lion faces the lion
text: The Sphinx looks due east, to the point where the sun rises at the spring and autumn equinoxes. Because the Earth's axis slowly wobbles, the constellation standing behind that sunrise changes, one sign in about 2,150 years. Today it is Pisces. In Khafre's day it was Taurus, the bull.

Hancock and Bauval point out that around 10,500 BCE the constellation on the equinox horizon was Leo, the lion. A lion-bodied monument facing the dawn of the Age of the Lion is, they argue, the plateau telling us when it was laid out.
Here at its paws, watch Khafre's king's head give way to the lion the First Time proposes, looking out past you to where Leo rose.
stops.numbers: The lion is a visual stand-in fitted to the Sphinx's surveyed outline. From the project's sky engine: at the spring equinox of 10,500 BCE the sun rose at 89°31′, with Regulus, Leo's brightest star, clearing the horizon 50 minutes ahead of it, 10°14′ south of due east.

more.label: Leo on the dawn horizon, drawn

stops.who: Hancock and Bauval, Keeper of Genesis (1996)

stops.summary: Bauval's correlation, with the belt at its lowest in 10,450 BCE.
stops.title: Orion's belt on the ground
text: In 1994 Robert Bauval proposed that the three pyramids are laid out as the three stars of Orion's belt: two bright stars nearly in line and a fainter third set off to one side, as Menkaure's smaller pyramid is set off the line of the other two. To the Egyptians Orion was Osiris, god of death and rebirth.

As the sky precesses, the belt climbs and sinks over a cycle of some 26,000 years. Watch it sink from 2450 BCE to 10,450 BCE, when it stood at its lowest. That, Bauval and Hancock argue, is the moment the ground plan records: the belt at the start of its cycle, set down in stone.
stops.numbers: Fitted on the ground, the three stars land 7.5, 14.9 and 7.4 m from the pyramids' centres across 936 m, once the belt is turned 13° to match. In 10,450 BCE Alnitak crossed the meridian 9°13′ above the horizon.

more.label: The belt fitted to the plan

stops.who: Bauval and Gilbert, The Orion Mystery (1994) · Hancock and Bauval (1996)

stops.summary: Four shafts, four stars, and two dates for one building.
stops.title: Shafts aimed at the stars
text: Two narrow shafts climb from the King's Chamber through the masonry to the open air, one north and one south, and two more rise from the Queen's Chamber below. The small dark square low in the south wall in front of you is the mouth of the southern shaft. In 1964 the astronomer Virginia Trimble and the architect Alexander Badawy showed that the southern shaft here pointed at Orion's belt as it crossed the meridian.
Rudolf Gantenbrink's robot surveyed the shafts in 1993, and Bauval matched all four: Orion's belt and Sirius to the south, Thuban, the pole star of its age, and Kochab to the north.

The case now runs on two clocks. The shafts date the building to around 2450 BCE; the plan on the ground records the sky of 10,450 BCE. Bauval reads them together: a monument built to remember an older moment, its First Time.
stops.numbers: Around 2450 BCE each star crosses within 0°40′ of its shaft: Alnitak 0°12′, Sirius 0°15′, Kochab 0°14′, Thuban 0°39′.

more.label: The four shafts and their stars

stops.who: Badawy and Trimble (1964) · Gantenbrink (1993) · Bauval and Gilbert (1994)

stops.summary: True north, pi and the 1:43,200 scale of the Earth.
stops.title: The shape of the Earth
text: The Great Pyramid's sides run within four arcminutes of true north, about a fifteenth of a degree. Its proportions are as exact: the perimeter of its base over its height is two times pi, to three hundredths of one per cent.

Hancock takes the next step. Multiply the height by 43,200 and you have the Earth's polar radius; the perimeter by 43,200, and you have the equator. And 43,200 is a number of the sky's own clock: the equinox moves one degree in about 72 years, and 43,200 is 600 times 72. On this reading the pyramid is a model of the northern hemisphere, drawn to the scale of precession.
stops.numbers: True north: 3′54″ off (Cole and Dash surveys). Perimeter over height: 6.2850 against 2π, 6.2832. Height × 43,200: 6,333 km against a polar radius of 6,357 km. Perimeter × 43,200: 39,801 km against an equator of 40,075 km.
stops.who: Hancock (1995) · Tompkins, Secrets of the Great Pyramid, with Stecchini (1971)

stops.summary: The Younger Dryas, Göbekli Tepe and a lost chapter of history.
stops.title: A lost chapter
text: Hancock's larger argument is that these clues point to a civilisation lost at the end of the last Ice Age. The Younger Dryas, about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago, swung the climate violently, and as the ice sheets melted the seas rose by more than a hundred metres, drowning the coasts where people lived. The survivors, he proposes, carried their knowledge of the sky to those who came after.

What was once easy to dismiss became harder in 1995, when Klaus Schmidt began to excavate Göbekli Tepe in Turkey: great carved stone pillars raised around 9500 BCE, thousands of years before the first cities. Monumental building at the date of the First Time is no longer unthinkable.
Now walk the plateau yourself. Every station can be seen in every era it was rendered in.
stops.who: Hancock, Magicians of the Gods (2015) · Schmidt, Göbekli Tepe excavations (from 1995)
